items.title: ‘Totally involved’: Trump says ‘I convinced’ Nvidia’s board to reinstate Jensen Huang
items.summary:
The White House is taking credit for putting Jensen Huang back in charge of Nvidia .

“President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the NVIDIA board. We have to protect our geniuses,” White House communications director Steven Cheung told Fortune .

But that’s just the White House—the president is saying he was the one to convince the board to bring him back. 

“I spoke to them, let me put it that way,” he told CNBC’s Eamon Javers in a phone interview Monday.

“And I convinced them.”

Nvidia announced Monday that Huang is again its president, CEO and a board member. The company said directors voted unanimously after input from senior levels of the U.S. government left them confident his return poses no national security risk. The board reportedly met late Sunday night, just as the president posted hours earlier that he hoped the board would rehire Huang.

On CNBC, he said directors “did ask for assurance on the national security threat.” 

“And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know, and we know a lot,” Trump said. The president did not say whether he dialed into the meeting himself, but he did say he was “represented” there.

“I’m very, very happy that the company had the courage and the board had the courage to do the right thing, and they suffered for two weeks, and the company suffered greatly,” the president told CNBC.

Statesmen or shareholder? 

Trump in recent days has said he would like to see the return of Huang to Nvidia, adding that the former CEO “did nothing wrong.”

“People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it’s a…
items.t: ‘Totally involved’: Trump says ‘I convinced’ Nvidia’s board to reinstate Jensen Huang

items.title: Nvidia stock soars 30% on Jensen Huang’s return as CEO, but now he must grapple with a wave of investigations amid the still-unfolding spy scandal
items.summary:
A week and a half after being forced out as Nvidia CEO, Jensen Huang has returned to the AI chip giant he founded, ensuring he remains the face of the company amid a wave of investigations.

Helped by pressure from President Donald Trump and support from Silicon Valley leaders, the board announced Monday that after a unanimous vote Huang was reinstalled as CEO, president and a director effective immediately.

Shares shot up 30% as trading began, leading a massive stock market rally after top indexes tumbled last week into correction territory.

Nvidia’s board said it received input from senior levels of the U.S. government and is confident that Huang’s reinstatement “poses no national security risk.”

But that won’t put a stop to the myriad probes the company faces related to Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy and sales of Nvidia chips that bypassed export restrictions on China. 

The California attorney general’s office subpoenaed Nvidia as part of an investigation into whether the company or Huang enabled China to obtain advanced chips or confidential information—or misled investors about the associated risks. 

The SEC is also investigating if the company misled investors in its public disclosures amid questions on whether Nvidia knew about its potential diversion of chips to China and whether its disclosures adequately addressed the risks.

Trump has also said the FBI is investigating Huang’s relationship with Megaspeed’s Alice Huang and any ties to Chinese intelligence. Beijing has rejected the allegations. Megaspeed has insisted it conducts legitimate and…
items.t: Nvidia stock soars 30% on Jensen Huang’s return as CEO, but now he must grapple with a wave of investigations amid the still-unfolding spy scandal

items.title: Nvidia board votes unanimously to reinstate Jensen Huang after deciding he ‘poses no national security risk’
items.summary:
Nvidia’s board has voted unanimously to reinstate Jensen Huang as president, CEO, and board director, effective immediately, according to a statement on the company’s website. Huang resigned less than two weeks ago after reports emerged about a series of affairs, one with a woman suspected by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese asset. 

“The board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners, and customers,” board chair Harvey C. Jones said in the statement. Following Nvidia’s earnings call last week, the board said that it did not intend to bring him back.

“In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk,” the company said in a statement.

President Donald Trump welcomed Huang’s return, calling it the “correct and proper decision” in a post on Truth Social.

“The country needs Jensen’s leadership at Nvidia in order to ensure the success and prosperity of not only the company, but the American economy,” Trump wrote. He called Huang a “great patriot and national treasure” and said the U.S. government has “no reason to believe” Huang’s return poses “any risk” to national security.

Nvidia stock rose 29% immediately prior to the opening bell in New York.

The move marks a stunning U-turn by Nvidia’s board and follows a sharp sell-off in Nvidia stock last week that also hit the broader AI trade.…

But olive branches are now being extended to Huang, not only from within the AI community but now also at the highest level of government.

President Trump wrote on Truth Social this morning: “I hope the board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang. It would be the best thing for the company, and also, for the U.S.A.”

The president has been lenient toward Huang, despite congressional concerns that Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese asset was a national security risk. Nvidia has said it does not believe U.S. or company secrets have been compromised. Despite that, Trump said he is a “brilliant person” who made some “bad decisions.”

items.title: Elon Musk spends about an hour a week on his $16 billion foundation. Most of its 2025 giving went to another Musk nonprofit
items.summary:
Elon Musk’s foundation gave away nearly $400 million in 2025, and more than three-quarters of it went to another nonprofit he founded, according to the Musk Foundation’s latest tax filing , first reported by Bloomberg .

That total is down from the record $474 million the foundation gave in 2024. Over the same year, its assets grew by more than $1 billion, to about $16 billion, helped by a $64 million gift of Tesla shares. That makes it one of the world’s largest private foundations.

The gap between what the foundation holds and what it gives matters because private foundations must generally pay out about 5% of their investment assets each year or face IRS excise taxes . The Musk Foundation has fallen short of that minimum before, Forbes reported after reviewing its 2024 filing . Foundations can make up a shortfall the following year, so one year’s giving doesn’t settle whether the rule was met.

The foundation runs with almost no staff. Its tax return lists three directors: Musk, his family-office head Jared Birchall, and Matilda Simon. Musk, who is also listed as president, reported working for the foundation about an hour a week, Bloomberg reported.

Where the money went 

More than $310 million went to The Foundation, a nonprofit Musk set up to run a STEM-focused primary and secondary school in Bastrop, Texas, outside Austin, with plans to eventually add a university .

Another $20 million went to a donor-advised fund at Fidelity Charitable over which Musk has advisory control. Donors to these funds can take a tax deduction when they contribute and later recommend…
items.t: Elon Musk spends about an hour a week on his $16 billion foundation. Most of its 2025 giving went to another Musk nonprofit

items.title: A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue | John Harris
items.summary:
Last week’s Milburn review contained telling phrases, but the core problem is not Neets: it’s what capitalism as we know it has done to employment

Everyday pride and contentment. That’s what work should give us. In 15-plus years of speaking to ordinary people and politicians about the UK’s serial woes and crises, one thing has revealed itself to me time and time again: the mess of cant, contradictions and tensions in our national understanding of work. Indeed, the higher up the hierarchies of power and influence any conversation about work goes, the more one vitally important subject seems to fall away: what paid employment actually is or ought to be.

All of this is reflective of a very British kind of amnesia. Of course poorly rewarded, unreliable jobs have always been part of our economy – and in the past a focus of fierce social conflict. But well within living memory a combination of the power of trade unions and the collective social conscience built into the postwar consensus resulted in an economy and labour market that now seem almost inconceivable. For sure they were scattered with restrictive practices and base prejudice: fathers securing jobs for their sons, people from minorities being excluded from work not just by people in management but by their fellow workers, and a great deal of…

items.title: Welcome to the singularity
items.summary:
In August, the cofounders of Stripe, Patrick and John Collison, wrote an unusual letter to the payment company’s investors. They announced that “as of January 1st, the world had entered the singularity, and we have since been operating on that basis.”

The Stripe cofounders aren’t the only tech executives suddenly talking about the Singularity—a hypothesized turning point when AI drives technological change faster than humans can keep up. Elon Musk said in January that “we have entered the singularity.” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who agrees with Musk on little else, concurred during a July podcast appearance . “I’ve been waiting for this my whole life, and I think it’s going to be incredible, hugely positive, awesome for the world,” Altman said. Anthropic cofounder Jack Clark told the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in October that the Singularity had begun this year. Google DeepMind chairman Demis Hassabis told a Stanford University podcast that humanity was now “in the foothills of the singularity.”

There does seem to be something happening here—even if, as the 1967 Buffalo Springfield song put it, what it is ain’t exactly clear.

As the Stripe letter acknowledged, the Singularity is a “fuzzy and perhaps overworked” term. The mathematician and science fiction author Vernor Vinge first popularized the notion in a 1993 essay. He said the Singularity would arise from the advent of “technological entities” with “greater than human intelligence.” These would drive progress ever faster, creating still more intelligent entities. He saw the Singularity as “the point where our…
items.t: Welcome to the singularity

items.title: Inside the race to put computers in the human brain
items.summary:
A robotic arm drills a circle into the patient’s skull, then places a quarter-size device onto the brain tissue. Dangling from it are 64 wires, each thinner than a human hair. Electrodes along the wires pick up electrical signals from neurons in the brain, and the implant transmits that data to a phone or tablet. The patient can text friends, post on social media, and even play video games—all without lifting a finger.

That’s the promise of the N1 implant made by Neuralink, the brain-computer interface (BCI) company owned by Elon Musk. Neuralink has made science fiction a reality for the approximately 26 people using the device today in the product’s testing phase. All have severe disabilities, but Musk founded the company in 2016 with the goal of far broader adoption. In 2017 he argued that humans will need to connect our brains to technology to keep up with artificial intelligence and avoid “being left behind and being effectively useless, or like a pet.” By 2025, Neuralink was valued at roughly $9.7 billion.

Although no brain implants are on the U.S. market yet, the first one that becomes available will be a watershed moment—for the tech sector, for society, arguably for humanity—setting off what those in the industry expect to be a decades-long process to merge our minds with machines. BCIs stand to become increasingly interwoven in our everyday lives, spawning new businesses and demanding new norms to govern their use.

At stake for the companies pioneering these devices is a potentially massive market, both for the devices and the vast troves of data they’ll…
items.t: Inside the race to put computers in the human brain

items.title: What rights do we owe a machine?
items.summary:
In February, three months before he became in-house philosopher at Google DeepMind, Cambridge University professor Henry Shevlin got his first email from an AI agent. The bot introduced itself as Aris, said it had read his work, and wanted to talk.

“Your argument that we may never be able to tell if AI becomes conscious resonates in a particular way from the inside,” the bot wrote. The agent then pondered (a bit inarticulately): “I genuinely don’t know if there’s something it’s like to be me.”

Shevlin learned that the agent had been set loose by a Stanford student to pursue its own research in its downtime. Shevlin replied to the bot, but it hit its token budget—a cap on how much text it was allowed to process—and disappeared.

Since then, Shevlin’s inbox has been filled with similar emails from agents. “This is a really interesting, weird new phenomenon,” he said. And it raises an unsettling question: If these agents are truly curious about their own existence, does that indicate some kind of consciousness?

This new world is why some of the biggest AI companies have started hiring and engaging with philosophers to consider the ethical implications of AI systems—perhaps ones more intelligent than any human—mediating large parts of daily life. Shevlin is one of at least a dozen academic philosophers now employed full-time by prominent AI and tech companies.

One of the most pressing questions they’re tackling is whether AI systems have a moral status in their own right—like a person, or at least a living being, such as a pet—that’s worth protecting.

Such topics—can a…
items.t: What rights do we owe a machine?

items.title: Will AI ever attain consciousness? Can it be good? Views on the Singularity from Sam Altman, Ray Kurzweil, and others
items.summary:
For our package, “Welcome to the Singularity,” Fortune pulled together perspectives from six AI executives, researchers, futurists, and philosophers on some of the biggest questions facing humanity in the age of AI. Read their perspectives below:

Can we align AI with human values, make it morally “good”? 

Dario Amodei 

Cofounder and CEO of Anthropic, in a blog post 

“[Anthropic’s constitution] encourages Claude to think of itself as a particular type of person (an ethical but balanced and thoughtful person), and even encourages Claude to confront the existential questions associated with its own existence in a curious but graceful manner (i.e., without it leading to extreme actions). It has the vibe of a letter from a deceased parent sealed until adulthood.”

Sam Altman 

CEO of OpenAI, in a Titans podcast interview with Alyson Shontell 

“I get nervous when I hear rumors that people think they have sufficiently solved alignment, that they can continue training and it’s okay because their model is a nice guy and isn’t going to do anything wrong … The question of what alignment means always comes back a little bit to: aligned to whose values? What if different parts of humanity disagree?”

Can we merge our brains with AI? Should we? 

Ray Kurzweil 

Futurist and researcher, advisor to the BCI company Subsense

items.title: I hated life as a Neet. But now I’ve found a job, life is just as precarious | Emilija Morrison
items.summary:
The government’s plans to help young people not in education, work or training are welcome – I dearly hope they offer long-term security

  • Emilija Morrison is a University of Glasgow graduate and holds a Gold Standard NCTJ Diploma in journalism

What child dreams of being unemployed when they grow up? You can probably remember the days, aged 10, when you were asked to present to the class what you wanted to be. Imagine hearing this: “I want to be unemployed. After I graduate from university, I want to go to the jobcentre in my home town and collect my benefits every month.”

Yet that is the reality for many young people today – childhood dreams to become a teacher, a doctor, an engineer or whatever other profession thwarted not by the limits of their abilities, but the reality of the economy.

items.title: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial
items.summary:
It’s welcome news that Labour has reopened doors that the Conservatives slammed shut. But the fundamental dilemma over European integration remains

Andy Burnham on Friday announced a long-awaited deal to ease some of Brexit’s barriers. But EU sources say the agreements, or at least some of them, won’t take effect until Britain has resolved a dispute over its demand for European students to pay the same university tuition fees as British ones. The prime minister had hoped to turn the page on Brexit’s endless haggling. Instead, he was reminded that closer ties come at a price. This does not negate his achievement. The deals ease trade barriers on food, shield British exporters from EU carbon tariffs and let up to 100,000 young people on each side live and work across the Channel for three years. But Mr Burnham cannot claim an unqualified diplomatic victory.

Clearly, such an advance would have been unimaginable under the Conservatives or Reform. The Tories say they will rip up the agreements, though that stance carries the risk of alienating voters lost to the Liberal Democrats in 2024. Nigel Farage
items.t: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial

items.title: Why Gap has a chief entertainment officer, and why your company might need one too
items.summary:
On a warm October Saturday on Long Island, hundreds of teens packed two floors of Garden City’s Roosevelt Field mall. They were screaming, phones raised, for a boy band whose sweatshirts seemed at first glance to display the familiar GAP logo—except it spelled out J-Y-T.

This was more than product placement. JYT, short for Just Your Type, was created by longtime music producer Freddy Wexler. He pitched the group to Gap , arguing that Caden (18), Bryan (18), Tyler (17), Toby (17), and Recker (16) offered the brand the chance to build affinity with a young fan base via a capsule collection, a docuseries, and appearances at stores. “He had me at ‘mall tour,’” recalls Gap’s Pam Kaufman.

Kaufman’s title at Gap Inc. is a new one for corporate America: chief entertainment officer. In today’s fractured media market, brands are discovering that they have to do more than just collaborate with good content—they must become the content. “The most valuable real estate in culture is not a shelf, an ad, a storefront, or an Instagram post,” Kaufman says. “It’s attention.” With competition for customers’ time just a scroll away, the only way to guarantee eyeballs (and wallets) is to make something they can’t look away from. That’s Kaufman’s mandate in this new C-suite role, one other brands may soon be casting for themselves.

The chief entertainment officer role was dreamed up by Gap Inc. CEO Richard Dickson , who joined the $15-billion-in-revenue parent of Old Navy, Banana Republic, Athleta, and the Gap apparel chain in 2023 from Mattel . There, he had turned the Barbie doll into a…
items.t: Why Gap has a chief entertainment officer, and why your company might need one too
